extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers of humour and satire; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance (early-18th-century) on composing and judging humorous and satirical prose: what counts as true humour vs false humour, the ethical limits and public aims of satire, and allied remarks on taste and beauty. Emphasizes reason, generality of targets, and moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour must lie under the check of Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour should always lie under the check of Reason; it requires the direction of the nicest judgment even as it indulges in the boundless freedoms of caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that many who call themselves humourists produce 'raving incoherent Pieces' that are 'rather the Offsprings of a Distempered Brain than Works of Humour.' Good humour balances freedom with rational control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity of thought (structure) in humour
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a kind of Nature and a certain Regularity of Thought which must discover the Writer to be a Man of Sense, even when he allows caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour should show an underlying order so the reader perceives intelligence behind the caprice; delirious mirth without structure elicits pity, not genuine laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: True humour is descended from Truth and Good Sense (wit + mirth)
rubrics_metrics.description: True Humour is presented as the offspring of Truth → Good Sense → Wit (married to Mirth) → HUMOUR: humour must be allied to truth and good sense and combine wit with mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genealogical metaphor indicates that humour lacking truth/good sense is spurious; effective humour mixes intelligent insight (wit) with playful spirit (mirth).

rubrics_metrics.name: True humour appears serious; false humour is ostentatiously laughing
rubrics_metrics.description: TRUE HUMOUR generally looks serious, whilst everybody laughs about him; FALSE HUMOUR is always laughing, whilst every body about him looks serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The surface tone matters: appearing too eager to provoke laughter signals imposture. Subtle, seemingly serious irony often produces more genuine communal amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of False Humour (hallmarks to avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: False Humour (the impostor) exhibits a cluster of vices: apish tricks and buffooneries; excessive mimickry indifferent to moral target; ridicules friends and foes alike ('bites the Hand that feeds him'); is void of reason and pursues no moral or instructive point; and its ridicule is personal (aimed at the man/writer rather than the vice or work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison enumerates five explicit features of false humour and compares it to a monkey rather than a man. Writers should avoid these signs—especially indiscriminate mimickry and personal lampooning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monstrous conceits and nonsense; nonsense is not humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Many writers mistake extravagant, irregular fancies and incoherent nonsense for humour; such 'monstrous Conceits' and raving incoherence are not humour but signs of a distempered brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good humour is not mere absurdity; it must be intelligible, attributable to judgment, and cognizant of moral or aesthetic limits. Examples: the author cites Shadwell’s plays and absurd modern pamphlets as cautionary instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should attack vices in the lump (multitudes), not individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator will 'scourge Vice and Folly as they appear in a Multitude... without condescending to be a Publisher of particular Intrigues and Cuckoldoms.' He promises never to draw a faulty character which does not fit at least a Thousand People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective and ethical satire targets general follies, fashions, or institutional vices rather than private scandals or single persons; this preserves benevolence and public usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/pubic purpose of satire: repress vices beyond law and pulpit
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper's use is to reprehend those Vices which are too trivial for the Chastisement of the Law, and too fantastical for the Cognizance of the Pulpit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire is justified as a public corrective: it should aim to reform or expose social follies that formal institutions cannot address. The tone should be benevolent and instructive rather than merely destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish private intrigues or intimate scandals
rubrics_metrics.description: The author explicitly disclaims being a 'Publisher of particular Intrigues and Cuckoldoms' and avoids exposing individual private matters for ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical limits: even when ridiculing vice, avoid airing intimate or defamatory particulars. Maintain decorum and focus on public vice, not private shame.

rubrics_metrics.name: When satirizing, aim at the Vice, not the Person
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule should be aimed at the Vice or the Writing, not at the Vicious Man or the Writer; personal mockery is a sign of false humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct criticism at conduct, fashions, or faulty texts; avoid vindictive or gratuitous attacks on individuals' characters or persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible exception: single out lampooners/libellers who produce ill-natured, immoral works
rubrics_metrics.description: Although generally attacking multitudes, the author allows an exception: to 'single out any of the small Wits, that infest the World with such Compositions as are ill-natured, immoral and absurd.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting persistent libellers and immoral lampooners is defended as retaliation and public service; such call-outs are treated as policing the public sphere rather than private spite.

rubrics_metrics.name: On theatrical and representational satire: expose affectation and 'monsters' of polite society
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatre should 'show no Monsters, but Men who are converted into such by their own Industry and Affectation' and represent 'unnatural Appearances which are in vogue among the Polite and Well-bred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic satire should demonstrate how affectation and fashion deform human behaviour; stage caricature should be illustrative of social causes (affectation, vanity), not gratuitous spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty (adjacent standard): true beauty is embellished by virtuous qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'true Art of assisting Beauty consists in Embellishing the whole Person by the proper Ornaments of virtuous and commendable Qualities' — virtues (innocence, piety, good humour, truth) beautify the person beyond mere physical features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portrayals (or judgments) of beauty, emphasize moral and intellectual qualities as what gives features their power to charm; external decoration (painted colours) may entertain the eye but cannot affect the heart.
